market_context: United States and Canada; household removal of food grease stains from washable clothing with pretreatment and a pre-dryer inspection.
title: How to Remove Grease Stains From Clothes

seo.title: How to Remove Grease Stains From Clothes
seo.meta_description: Lift away food, blot surface grease, pretreat with liquid detergent, wash by the care label, and check the stain before drying.
seo.search_intent: Remove food grease stains from clothing without spreading them, setting residue with heat, or damaging the fabric.

excerpt: Lift away food and surface grease first, pretreat the spot with liquid laundry detergent or a fabric-safe grease remover, and wash according to the care label. Check the area before using the dryer. Sauces may need a second treatment because they can leave pigment or protein behind after the grease is gone.
content_html:
A grease stain from dinner is often more complicated than it looks. Butter, gravy, frying fat, salad dressing, or a creamy sauce can leave oil plus pigments, proteins, or sugar. That is why a spot may lose its greasy feel but still leave a colored mark behind.

The reliable approach is to lift away excess food, pretreat the greasy area, wash according to the care label, and inspect before applying dryer heat.

Remove solids and surface grease first

Lift off sauce, butter, or food with a spoon or dull edge. Then blot gently with a clean cloth or paper towel.

Avoid rubbing outward. That can spread a compact stain into a larger ring.

Let the garment label set the limits

Washable cotton can tolerate treatments that silk, wool, embellished items, or dry-clean-only garments may not. Check the care label before choosing water temperature or stain product.

For delicate or professionally cleaned garments, prompt professional treatment may be safer than experimenting at home.

Pretreat with a laundry product designed to handle grease

Apply liquid laundry detergent or a grease-compatible fabric stain remover and work it in gently. The American Cleaning Institute recommends pretreating oily and greasy stains before laundering.

Follow the product's contact-time directions rather than leaving it on indefinitely.

Sauces can leave two stains in one

Mayonnaise is mostly a grease problem. Tomato sauce with oil combines fat and pigment. Creamy sauces may also contain protein. If the dark oily halo disappears but color remains, treat the remaining component with a product that is safe for the fabric.

This is why one pass does not always solve a food stain completely.

Dish soap is not a universal clothing treatment

Hand dishwashing liquid is good at cutting grease, but it is not formulated for every fabric, finish, washer, or color. Laundry detergent or a textile stain remover is usually a more predictable starting point.

If a garment manufacturer specifically allows another method, use only a small amount and rinse thoroughly before machine washing.

Wash for the fabric, not for your frustration level

Choose the warmest water and strongest cycle the care label safely allows. That may still mean cold water and a gentle cycle.

Removing the stain is not a success if the garment shrinks or loses color in the process.

Inspect before tumble drying

Look at the area while the item is still damp. A greasy residue often appears as a darker patch.

If you see it, pretreat and wash again. Dryer heat can make remaining grease much more stubborn.

A dried-in stain may still respond

Re-wet the area, apply a compatible grease treatment, allow the labeled contact time, and wash again. Old stains often need repeated moderate treatment.

Avoid mixing cleaning chemicals to make a stronger formula; that can damage fabric and may create unsafe reactions.

If the spill happens away from home, do less rather than more

At a restaurant or work, lift off food and blot with a clean napkin. Avoid salt, hand sanitizer, perfume, or whatever cleaning product happens to be nearby unless the garment maker specifically recommends it.

A small, controlled first response is better than spreading grease or damaging color before proper pretreatment is available.

Synthetic fabrics can hold grease stubbornly

Polyester and other synthetics readily retain oily soils. If the garment is washable and the spot survives one cycle, repeat the grease pretreatment rather than increasing water or dryer temperature beyond the care label.

Give athletic and synthetic items enough room in the washer so detergent and rinse water can move through the fabric.

When the appearance is clean but odor remains

Clothing heavily exposed to cooking grease can smell oily even after the visible stain disappears. Rewash with the correct detergent dose and avoid overloading the washer so the item can rinse properly.

Grease removal is less about attacking the stain and more about giving detergent enough contact with the oily residue to carry it away. Early treatment and no dryer heat until the spot is gone make the biggest difference.

faq.question: How do I treat a fresh grease stain?
faq.answer: Lift off excess food, blot surface grease, pretreat with liquid laundry detergent, and wash according to the garment label.

faq.question: Should I use dish soap on clothes?
faq.answer: Not as a universal rule. Laundry detergent or a fabric stain remover is a more predictable choice for clothing.

faq.question: Why is there still color after the oily mark is gone?
faq.answer: Sauces often contain pigments, proteins, or spices in addition to fat, so a second type of stain may remain.

faq.question: What if I already dried the stain?
faq.answer: Re-wet, pretreat, and wash it again. Heat can make grease more stubborn, so repeated treatment may be necessary.
